name: Vaccinium arctostaphylos (Caucasian whortleberry)
short: Thin evidence: small 2-3 month trials (37-50 per group) in high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes or high lipids, 3 of 4 on medicines: no adverse effects; blood pressure, glucose fell more than placebo.
text: Safety evidence is limited to a few small, short placebo-controlled trials, which reported no harms. In 100 overweight or obese people with high blood pressure taking standard blood pressure medicines, 3 months of a berry extract taken by mouth lowered systolic and diastolic blood pressure more than placebo (systolic readings fell from 152.1 to 140.5 with the extract and from 152.9 to 150.8 with placebo) and had no significant effect on blood counts or liver and kidney tests, and the authors observed no side effects and no adverse interaction with the other blood pressure drugs. In 74 people with type 2 diabetes taking glucose-lowering drugs, 2 months of a fruit extract lowered fasting and 2-hour after-meal blood glucose and HbA1c more than placebo, with no significant effect on liver or kidney function, and no adverse effects were reported; in 80 people with high blood lipids, 2 months of a fruit extract had no significant effect on liver enzymes or creatinine and no adverse effects were reported. A 2-month trial of a leaf extract (a different plant part) in 100 people with high blood pressure, high blood lipids and type 2 diabetes taking conventional drugs found that the extract lowered fasting and after-meal glucose, HbA1c and systolic and diastolic blood pressure more than placebo, and reported no adverse effects and no significant effects on liver enzymes or creatinine. None of these abstracts reports low blood pressure or low blood sugar. The abstracts do not describe longer use or use in pregnancy. Apart from the one trial that observed no adverse interaction with blood pressure drugs, no interaction data were found in the cited sources.
